title: The Louis Theroux Effect
author: Jonny Thomson
summary: Philosopher Jonny Thomson begins with meeting documentary maker Louis Theroux and uses the encounter to describe what he calls the Louis Theroux Effect: we start talking, behaving, and thinking like those we spend time around. After binge-watching Theroux he found himself using his stock phrases and tolerating silences, which made him a better listener. He challenges the common self-help idea that changing beliefs comes first and behaviour follows, noting that there is little evidence we can switch beliefs on and off at will. Drawing on Xunzi and Confucian ritual, he argues that character is cultivated from the outside in through the books, experiences, and people we surround ourselves with. Priming and imitation, which Aristotle called natural to humans, are happening anyway, so we should deliberately choose who and what is doing the priming. The essay is a light but useful case for shaping habits by shaping environment and models.
points: We unconsciously absorb the speech, habits, and ways of listening of the people and media we spend time with.
Deliberately imitating a skilled listener, such as letting silences run a few seconds longer, can improve your own listening.
The belief-first model of self-improvement is doubtful because people lack direct voluntary control over what they believe.
Xunzi's view is that character is built from the outside in, through surrounding yourself with good books, experiences, and people.
Since priming and imitation occur regardless, the sensible move is to choose your models and environment on purpose.
quotes: It turns out that when you stop scrambling around for things to say, you can actually listen much better.
I’ve since called this the “Louis Theroux Effect” — which is the tendency I think we all have to start talking, behaving, and even thinking like those we spend a lot of time around.

To change your inner life, you have to change your outer life. In the modern psychological lexicon, we talk about behavioral activation or self-perception theory, but this idea appears far earlier than that.

The third-century B.C. philosopher Xunzi argued that character is something we cultivate from the outside in. You cannot turn on patience, bravery, or temperance like an RPG character at a level-up screen.
Instead, we have to surround ourselves with good books, good experiences, and good people, and over time that works its way into our being.
This is called “priming” in some contexts, or “leading” in others. But we are all being primed and led all the time.
Let yourself be led and let yourself be primed because it’s happening anyway. And you might as well take some control over who’s doing the priming.
